'''Geoffrey Ainsworth Harrison''' [[Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland|FRAI]] (8 June 1927 – 14 September 2017) was an English biological anthropologist who taught at the [[University of Oxford]].

==Early life and education==
Harrison was born in [[Teddington]], [[Middlesex]], [[England]], on 8 June 1927. He received a 1st class degree from [[Trinity College, Cambridge]], where he read natural sciences. At Cambridge, he became interested in [[anthropology]] after attending a lecture on ''[[Australopithecus]]'' by paleontologist [[Robert Broom]].<ref name=news>{{Cite web |url=http://www.anthropology-news.org/index.php/2017/10/27/geoffrey-ainsworth-harrison/ |title=Geoffrey Ainsworth Harrison |last=Little |first=Michael A. |date=2017-10-27 |website=Anthropology News |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171103001352/http://www.anthropology-news.org/index.php/2017/10/27/geoffrey-ainsworth-harrison/ |archive-date=2017-11-03 |access-date=2018-05-06}}</ref> He received his [[DPhil]] from the University of Oxford for his work on the adaptation of mice to warm environments, which he conducted under the supervision of [[Joseph Weiner]].<ref name=obit>{{Cite web |url=http://www.parkesfoundation.org.uk/images/Harrison%20obituary%20November%202017.pdf |title=Geoffrey Ainsworth Harrison Obituary |website=Parkes Foundation}}</ref>

==Academic career==
Harrison's first academic position was as a lecturer at the [[University of Liverpool]], where he studied [[skin pigmentation]]. In 1963, he joined the faculty at Oxford as Reader in Physical Anthropology, where he was appointed Professor of Biological Anthropology in 1976.<ref name=news/><ref name=obit/> As a faculty member at Oxford, he was noted for his central role in the founding of the Human Sciences degree.<ref name=ihs>{{Cite web |url=https://www.ihs.ox.ac.uk/article/professor-geoffrey-ainsworth-harrison |title=Professor Geoffrey Ainsworth Harrison |website=Institute of Human Sciences |language=en |access-date=2018-05-06 |archive-date=2018-05-07 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180507085407/https://www.ihs.ox.ac.uk/article/professor-geoffrey-ainsworth-harrison |url-status=dead }}</ref> He also helped to establish Oxford's Diploma in Human Biology, the Department of Biological Anthropology (later the Institute of Biological Anthropology), and the MSc in Human Biology. He retired from Oxford in 1994, though he continued to write and conduct research for an additional 20 years.<ref name=news/> He received the [[Huxley Memorial Medal]] from the [[Royal Anthropological Institute of Great Britain and Ireland|Royal Anthropological Institute]] in 1987 for his work 'Social Heterogeneity and Biological Variation' although no papers on this are held by the institute.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Huxley Memorial Medal and Lecture Prior Recipients |url=https://www.therai.org.uk/awards/honours-prior-recipients/huxley-memorial-medal-and-lecture-prior-recipients/ |access-date=2022-04-02 |website=Royal Anthropological Institute |language=en-gb}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=HUXLEY MEMORIAL LECTURES (A115) |url=https://www.therai.org.uk/archives-and-manuscripts/archive-contents/huxley-memorial-lectures-a115/ |access-date=2022-04-02 |website=Royal Anthropological Institute |language=en-gb}}</ref>

==Professional affiliations==
Harrison was president of the [[Royal Anthropological Institute]] from 1969 to 1970.<ref name=ihs/> He was also chair of the [[Society for the Study of Human Biology]] and of the [[Biosocial Society]], as well as a member of many learned societies.<ref name=obit/>

==Death==
Harrison died in [[Oxford]], England, on 14 September 2017.<ref name=news/>
